title: Run first pre-annotation batch and begin gold annotation
description:
Run the first 100-turn Claude pre-annotation batch on the complete 20-dialogue corpus, review output quality, then begin gold annotation on a selected subset of 5-8 dialogues.

## Steps

### 1. Run pre-annotation batch
Uses python3.13 (python3 does not have anthropic installed).

```bash
python3.13 scripts/preannotate.py
```

Default batch size is 100 turns. Corpus has 279 turns total. The script will:
- Load the full aarc_taxonomy_v1.md into Claude's context (cached)
- Annotate turns sequentially using a trailing 7-turn causal window
- Print each turn's labels + confidence + rationale as it goes
- Save to data/pre_annotations.jsonl

Check progress at any time:
```bash
python3.13 scripts/preannotate.py --list
```

Run again for subsequent batches (script is idempotent — skips already-annotated turns).

### 2. Review pre-annotation quality
Inspect data/pre_annotations.jsonl to assess label quality and rationale quality before committing to gold annotation. Check deficit rate distribution and mean confidence from the --list output.

### 3. Select dialogues for gold annotation
Choose 5-8 dialogues that cover: all four deficit types, boundary cases, and a range of termination outcomes (resolution, impasse, breakdown). Identify scenario IDs from:
```bash
python3.13 -c "import json; [print(json.loads(l)['scenario_id'], json.loads(l)['termination_reason'], len(json.loads(l)['turns']), 'turns') for l in open('data/corpus.jsonl')]"
```

### 4. Run gold annotation session
```bash
python3.13 scripts/annotate.py --dialogues scenario-001,scenario-003,...
```

For each turn:
- Trailing 7-turn context is displayed, focal turn marked ►
- Claude's suggestion shown: labels (A/Ag/R/C), confidence, one-sentence rationale
- [Enter] = accept all Claude labels
- [a/g/r/c] = flip individual components (combinable, e.g. 'ar' flips A and R)
- [n] = add annotator note, then accept
- [s] = skip turn
- [?] = show help
- Ctrl+C = save progress and exit

Progress and deficit rates:
```bash
python3.13 scripts/annotate.py --list
```

### 5. Evaluate pre-annotation quality (after ~20 gold turns)
Once ~20 gold turns are annotated, compare against Claude's pre-annotations to estimate agreement. If agreement < 0.70, review the pre-annotator prompt and taxonomy loading before continuing.

## Acceptance criteria
- First 100 turns pre-annotated and saved to data/pre_annotations.jsonl
- Pre-annotation quality reviewed and deemed acceptable
- At least one gold annotation session started on selected dialogues
close_reason: Pre-annotation batch complete. 44 unreviewed turns redone + 50 new turns run with claude-opus-4-6 under v2 schema. Gold annotation at 56/100.

title: Annotate ~100 turns across corpus as gold standard (turn-level)
description:
Manually annotate approximately 100 turns across the corpus at the turn level, assigning binary deficit labels (yes/no) for each of the four AARC components per turn: Acknowledgement, Agency, Reciprocity, Clarity.

WHY 100 TURNS:
These gold annotations are not the reward model training data — they are the calibration and validation material for the LLM silver annotator. The silver annotator will process the remaining ~210 windows across the full corpus to produce the bulk of preference pairs needed for reward model training (~5,000–7,000 pairs at N=10 candidates per high-friction window). The gold annotations do three things:
1. Provide few-shot conditioning examples for the silver annotator (covering all deficit types and combinations)
2. Establish a held-out test set to verify the silver annotator meets the 70% agreement threshold before it is trusted on the full corpus
3. Produce a small tier of high-confidence gold preference pairs (~1,300–1,500 at N=10) that can be mixed with silver pairs at higher weight during reward model training

SELECTION CRITERIA:
Select turns to ensure coverage of all deficit types and combinations — prioritise dialogues that the researcher's review suggests contain clear examples of each AARC component deficit. Aim for 5–8 fully annotated dialogues rather than sparse sampling across all 20, so that window-level aggregation is coherent within each annotated dialogue.

WHAT HAPPENS NEXT:
1. Hold back ~20 annotated windows as a test set
2. Condition the LLM silver annotator on the remaining gold windows as few-shot examples
3. Run silver annotator on full corpus
4. Measure agreement between silver and held-out gold — must reach 70% before proceeding
5. If agreement < 70%, refine the rubric and re-annotate the edge cases
6. Once validated, generate N=10 candidate interventions per high-friction window across the full silver-annotated corpus to produce preference pairs for reward model training

DEPENDS ON: FPO-pcc (CLI refactor for turn-level annotation)
close_reason: 100 turns annotated across 9 transcripts (gold standard complete). LLM pre-annotations run on all matched turns. IAA baseline: mean κ=0.401 across 90 stable turns; b88cef11 batch (10 turns) shows poor LLM-human agreement, flagged for FPO-7ix investigation.

title: Refactor CLI annotation tool for turn-level deficit labeling
description:
The current annotation CLI (MOD-005) presents 7-turn windows and elicits one binary deficit label per AARC component per window. This needs to be refactored to present individual turns and elicit binary deficit labels per turn, so that window-level severity can be derived algorithmically as a count or density of deficits within the window rather than being assigned directly by the annotator.

Changes required:
- Present turns one at a time (or in short context, e.g. with 2 turns of context above and below) rather than full 7-turn windows
- For each turn, prompt for 4 binary labels: acknowledgement_deficit, agency_deficit, reciprocity_deficit, clarity_deficit (same components, same binary yes/no)
- Persist turn-level labels to a new data structure (DS-TL or extension of DS-009)
- Derive window-level deficit labels by aggregating turn-level labels within each 7-turn window: a window has a given deficit if any turn within it is labeled with that deficit; window severity = count of turns with that deficit
- Update is_high_friction to fire when any window deficit count >= 1
- Ensure the annotator can navigate forward/backward through turns and revise labels before finalising a dialogue
- Retain the ability to add a rationale note at the turn level

title: Corpus resolution bias: 19/20 dialogues terminate as resolution
description: The generated corpus shows near-uniform resolution (19/20), with no impasses or breakdowns. This is a known LLM tendency — models trained on helpfulness converge toward agreement even when personas should resist. A realistic corpus needs a distribution across resolution, impasse, and breakdown to produce varied friction windows and a meaningful reward signal. Levers to investigate: (1) tighten director prompt to resist premature closure, (2) raise min_turns from 8 to 12-14 to prevent quick resolutions, (3) strengthen persona activation profiles to make positions more entrenched, (4) raise the bar in the termination check for what counts as genuine resolution. Regeneration of the corpus will be needed once the fix is validated.
notes: Adversarial director prompt implemented in _DIRECTOR_SYSTEM (dialogue_generator.py). Director now explicitly tasked with preventing premature resolution: raises the bar for calling resolution verdict (requires both parties to explicitly acknowledge the other's core need AND reach concrete agreement), and injects anti-resolution directions when the scene softens (surface unacknowledged wounds, expose ambivalence under cooperative gestures, reactivate activation profiles). Fix not yet validated — see corpus regeneration issue.
close_reason: Resolved through persona schema enrichment (TKI modes, storm shift, face salience, repair orientation) and director profile awareness — outcome distribution now emerges from character dynamics rather than directorial manipulation. Validated: impasse at 8 turns on scenario 2 Casey/Sam.

title: Add taxonomy to DSPy MiPROv2 prompt and re-optimize
description:
MiPROv2 optimization without the taxonomy hits a ceiling on Clarity (F1=0.000 in medium run, F1=0.250 best case in light run) because the repair/deficit distinction cannot be learned from gold examples alone — the model needs the definitional grounding the taxonomy provides.

The fix: add taxonomy as a fixed InputField to AARCAnnotation signature. Structure becomes:
  [FIXED: taxonomy ~16K tokens] + [OPTIMIZED: MiPROv2 instructions] + [OPTIMIZED: 1-2 demos] + [VARIABLE: dialogue context]

MiPROv2 then optimizes instructions that work *together* with the taxonomy — targeting repair/deficit contrast specifically. This is directly analogous to the raw GPT-5.4 baseline (κ=0.413 on Clarity) but with optimized instructions layered on top.

Implementation:
1. Add taxonomy: str = dspy.InputField() to AARCAnnotationSignature in dspy_annotator.py
2. Store taxonomy_text in AARCAnnotator.__init__, pass in forward()
3. Build dspy.Example objects with taxonomy field included
4. Re-run light optimization with recall-weighted metric and val-size=70
5. Compare Clarity F1 vs raw GPT-5.4 baseline (κ=0.196) and best prior run (F1=0.250)

Cost note: each call ~16K tokens heavier; 2 demos adds ~34K tokens per call. Acceptable for a 140-turn IAA baseline run but worth noting for full-corpus scale.
close_reason: AGR-only medium MiPROv2 run completed. Ack F1=0.800 (near Claude ceiling), Rec F1=0.667 (above GPT baseline). Agency F1=0.250 regressed — confirmed definitional problem. Optimization track concluded; Claude remains primary annotator.

title: Optimize annotation pipeline with DSPy MiPROv2 and per-label macro-F1 metric
description: Once GPT baseline IAA is validated (FPO-xlg), build a DSPy-optimized annotation module using MiPROv2. Prior BootstrapFewShot/GPT-4o attempt yielded mean κ=0.391 with Clarity κ=0.274 due to a bidirectional repair/deficit confusion error and coarse optimization metric. MiPROv2 jointly optimizes instructions and demonstrations via Bayesian search. Use per-label macro-F1 computed at minibatch level as the primary optimization target (precedent: Saranathan et al. 2024, arXiv:2412.15298). Add per-component κ as a secondary diagnostic. If the F1-optimized model still exhibits the Clarity bidirectional error pattern, switch primary target to κ.
close_reason: MiPROv2 optimization runs completed (3 passes: light accuracy, medium accuracy, light recall-weighted). Best result: Macro-F1 0.505 on 40-turn val set. Clarity cannot be resolved without taxonomy in-context — superseded by FPO-59s.

title: Add pragmatic stylistics profiles as third generation input alongside personas and scenarios

Each profile defines four parameters: (1) Silence/Pauses — how the speaker treats silence (uncomfortable gap vs. thoughtful space); (2) Fillers/Discourse Markers — frequency and type of floor-holding sounds/phrases and their social interpretation; (3) Turn-Taking/Overlap — tolerance for interruption vs. strict wait-time (e.g., cooperative overlap vs. sequential); (4) Indirectness/Hedging — degree of directness vs. face-saving indirection. Profiles are passed into the agent's generation prompt alongside their Persona. When two agents receive clashing stylistic norms, this generates pragmatic friction on top of content-level conflict, enriching the deficit signal available for annotation. title: Corpus register bias: LLM-generated dialogues calibrated to metropolitan, educated, liberal communication norms
notes: The synthetic corpus production methodology is largely LLM-driven. LLMs reproduce dominant register patterns — likely a Western, educated, metropolitan, liberal (WEIRD-adjacent) communicative style. This limits corpus utility for cross-cultural mediation contexts where parties operate under significantly different communicative norms (e.g., First Nations mediations, intercultural disputes). The annotation schema and gold standard dialogues will implicitly encode these norms, potentially producing models that perform well in-distribution but fail or misfire in culturally distinct contexts. title: Validate synthetic corpus against naturalistic conflict data
description: The dialogue generation pipeline has not been empirically evaluated for how well it approximates real conflict interaction. Whether persona-scenario conditioned two-agent LLM dialogues capture the range and structure of naturalistic conflict dialogue — specifically for AARC deficit detection — rests on design reasoning rather than measurement. DiaSynth (Suresh et al., 2025) demonstrates 90.48% performance distribution capture in a general domain setting, but that result does not establish fitness for deficit detection in mediation-relevant conflict. A dedicated study is required: systematic comparison of the synthetic corpus against a reference set of naturalistic conflict transcripts, assessing whether deficit signal distribution, escalation trajectories, and stylistic variation are consistent with real interactions. Deferred to future work; data collection or licensing would be required.

title: Explore open model annotation via Ollama as cost-free inference alternative
description: Before committing to GPT + MiPROv2 as the optimized annotation pipeline, investigate whether a capable open model (e.g. Llama 3, Qwen, Mistral) running locally via Ollama can achieve acceptable IAA on the AARC taxonomy. Key question: can open models follow the deficit/repair distinction and boundary case discriminators well enough to meet the κ ≥ 0.40 threshold? If viable, unlimited local inference would eliminate annotation cost at scale. Scope: test one candidate model against the 140 gold turns using the same taxonomy prompt; compare per-component κ against GPT baseline.
notes: Hardware assessment complete (2026-05-07): No rate-limit issue — Ollama is purely hardware-bounded, unlike Groq. Critical gotcha: must set num_ctx=20000 per-request (Ollama defaults to 4K). OpenAI-compatible API, reuses gpt_annotator.py pattern with base_url swap + extra_body option. Hardware constraint on 24GB Mac Pro: Qwen2.5 32B needs ~24-26GB including KV cache at 16K context — too tight. Qwen2.5 14B (Q4, ~12-14GB) is the safe choice on this hardware. Recommended next step: pull qwen2.5:14b, run single test call with num_ctx=20000 to confirm memory headroom before committing to full 140-turn eval.
